newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says oil spill one-tenth earlier estimate.
newsitem.headline: Japan says oil spill one-tenth earlier estimate.

text.p: Embarrassed government officials said on Thursday that an oil spill from a supertanker in Tokyo Bay, initially thought to be of record proportions, was just one-tenth the size previously estimated.

Smarting from criticism about a slow response to an oil spill in western Japan in January, the government went into high gear on Wednesday after the Japanese-operated tanker Diamond Grace scraped a reef in shallow water, damaging three of its storage tanks.

A flotilla of more than 300 ships was summoned to fight the spill, which officials had estimated at 13,400 tonnes (100,000 barrels), which would have made it the biggest ever in Japan. But on Thursday, officials revised down the size of the spill to a more modest 1,315 tonnes (9,800 barrels).
"We don't know why there was such a huge discrepancy. But anyway it's better than what we had last night," a spokesman for the Maritime Safety Agency told Reuters.
Transport Minister Makoto Koga said: "I went to see the prime minister and the chief cabinet secretary to report and apologise for the big mistake."
Despite its smaller size, the slick still poses a threat to marine life in the area. Officials have said that given the sheltered nature of Tokyo Bay, the slick is unlikely to break up on its own.
By early Thursday it covered an area of the bay about 15 km by 18 km (9.4 miles by 11 miles), four times bigger than it had been on Wednesday afternoon.
The tanker, a very large crude carrier (VLCC), was carrying 257,000 tonnes (1.9 million barrels) of crude oil from the United Arab Emirates to a refinery in Kawasaki, south of Tokyo.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto declared the spill a national disaster and asked the police, coastguard, local governments and the Japanese and U.S. armed forces to help in the cleanup.
On Thursday he said that oil spilled from the third of the tanker's tanks "seems to have flowed into the second empty tank and miraculously didn't leak outside".
Shigehiro Sakamoto, head of rescue and security operations at the Yokohama regional coastguard, said officials were investigating the error in reporting the size of the slick.
He told a news conference the original figure was based on an estimate by Nippon Yusen KK, the operator of the ship.
Officials hinted that human error may have been responsible for the accident, which took place in an area with sophisticated navigation equipment and in calm seas.
"The pilot said the tanker did not suffer any mechanical or engine failure," coastguard operations coordinator Saburo Sunaga told a news conference.
The pilot, Seiji Ushio, 57, who was on board, had also told the coastguard that the tanker had not been trying to avoid a collision with another ship.
"So we suspect the accident was caused by some form of human error," Sunaga said.
The single-hull tanker, built in 1994, was chartered by Mitsubishi Oil and operated by a subsidiary of Nippon Yusen, Japan's largest shipping company.
Many recently built tankers have double hulls, meant to reduce the chances of an oil spill in case of an accident. Double hulls are compulsory for ships built since 1996.
Under an international convention, there is automatic insurance of up to $194 million for large vessels, with the operator or shipowner primarily responsible for the rest.
Late on Wednesday, the tanker left the scene of the accident under its own power and docked at its original destination near Tokyo.

Japan's worst oil spill was in November 1971, when a tanker spilled 6,000 tonnes of crude oil into Niigata Bay. In January's incident in western Japan, about 5,200 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled from the capsized Russian tanker Nakhodka.
